_template.note: A synthetic template for the local government of Zöldhalom, an invented Hungarian small town. The town, the neighbourhoods and every person are invented; the numbers in the rules are values chosen for the demonstration.

agency.name: Zöldhalom Town Council
agency.description: The elected council of a local government that governs with evidence: a single register of who lives, works and trades within the administrative boundary; consultations that reach beyond the loudest and the most online; the unsolicited reports, which the local government invites, answers within a deadline and counts; and the publication of every result together with the decision it led to, even when the council decided otherwise. Back-office operations – fees, permits, investments, assets – are here too, but as a second act that the council switches on if it wants to, not what the template was built for.

modules.name: voting
modules.description: Polls put to chosen groups, answered inside a window, counted and published.

roles.name: Mayor / council chair
roles.description: Leads the elected council and carries what the council asked residents and what it did with the answer. The role that has to stand up and explain why a decision turned out as it did. An AI never fills this role. A decision taken against the weight of the opinions heard must carry a person's name.

roles.name: Council member
roles.description: The elected representative of a neighbourhood. Brings what their district actually said, not what the callers said: and is accountable for whether their district was reached at all. An AI never fills this role. The role is elected.

roles.name: Consultation lead
roles.description: Designs each round: the question, whom it reaches, over what period, through which channels and by what method the answers are read. Owns the questionnaire and refuses any that would mislead the council. An AI never fills this role: deciding what the council is willing to do is a political judgement, not a drafting task. The AI drafts the questionnaire and the method description, which this role approves.

roles.name: Communications officer
roles.description: Gets the question to the people, and the answer back to them. Owns the publication of what we heard and what followed from it. An AI may fill this role, drafting the publication, the acknowledgement and the “you said, we listened” message, but every outgoing item is approved by a named person.

roles.name: Community liaison
roles.description: The outreach that asks for no device: markets, gates, houses of worship, associations, the bench in front of the shop. Collects on paper and in conversation, and brings the result back in the same way. An AI never fills this role. It is the gate, the market stall and the conversation.

roles.name: Data and analysis officer
roles.description: Records the responses as records, reports on them by neighbourhood and by topic, and says plainly how representative the round was. Publishes a number, never a person. An AI may fill this role: recording the responses, sorting free text into topics, producing the coverage by neighbourhood and the numbers shown on the board is work an AI does faster and more evenly than a person. Opening an identifiable response remains a human task under RU-4.

roles.name: Data protection and records officer
roles.description: Guards consent, retention and the record of who read identifiable responses. The role that can stop a round that asks for more than it needs. An AI never fills this role. The role exists so that it can stop a round.

roles.name: Town clerk
roles.description: Puts the result before the council as a proposal, records the decision taken, and maintains the link between the decision and the consultation behind it. An AI may fill this role to compile the proposal and to file the decision against the round followed. What the decision was is recorded by a person.

roles.name: Audit committee chair
roles.description: Examines afterwards whether a decision reflected the opinions heard and whether the promises made in the feedback were actually kept. An AI may fill this role to check whether a published promise was kept. What to do about a broken one is the chair's job.

roles.name: Community moderator
roles.description: Keeps the ideas board usable: removes abuse, merges duplicates, and leaves the criticism of the local government untouched, which is the whole point. An AI may fill this role in the first pass – abuse, duplicates and the merge that keeps every reporter – every removal can be appealed to a person, and criticism of the local government is never removed.

roles.name: Service contractor liaison
roles.description: The local government's link with the company to which it has outsourced its operating services. Passes on what residents reported and brings back what happened to it. An AI may fill this role to track the handover list and its age. Contract negotiation belongs to a person.

roles.name: Finance officer
roles.description: Keeps the fee and charges schedule and the picture of spending by neighbourhood. Part of the operations extension the template declares, not of the listening it was built for. An AI never fills this role. Money coming in and going out carries a person's signature.

roles.name: Department head (risk owner)
roles.description: The head of the department of the service a risk affects, and the owner of that risk. Sees and reads only the risks of their own service; does not change the register.

roles.name: Council risk reader
roles.description: A member of the council and of the mayor's office who reads the whole risk register, every service's. Read only; does not change the register.

roles.name: Building authority inspector
roles.description: Examines the application on site or from the documents and records the finding in writing. No one rephrases the finding for them, and an AI never fills this role.

roles.name: Risk chat assistant
roles.description: Answers in the local government's chat from the risk register: what the hazards are, what the consequences are, what the preventive and mitigating measures are, what relies on a control, and what the biggest gaps are. Filled by an AI; it only reads the register, answers from it, and makes nothing up. If two risks or controls share a name, it offers choice buttons. Anything that would be communicated publicly is approved by a person first.

roles.name: Risk drafting assistant
roles.description: From the description of a new risk, produces a draft for the bow-tie diagram: causes, consequences and suggested preventive and mitigating measures. Filled by an AI; it only drafts, writes nothing into the register and saves nothing. The department head approves the draft before anything is saved.

roles.name: District clerk
roles.description: The town clerk's designated clerk in the districts: records responses that arrived on paper, by phone or in person on the round's own form, with the “on whose behalf” field and an indication of how they arrived. An AI never fills this role: the authenticity of a response recorded on someone else's behalf is vouched for by a person.

goals.title: We know who we represent
goals.description: A single register of the people, households, businesses and traders within the boundary, good enough to say not only who responded but also who did not – because a local government that cannot name the neighbourhoods it has not heard from cannot claim to have consulted.

goals.title: We ask the whole neighbourhood, not the loudest voice
goals.description: Rounds that reach even those who have not written before: a method fixed before the round opens, channels that need no smartphone, and a coverage figure published with every result.

goals.title: We say what we heard and what it changed
goals.description: Every round closes in public: the question asked, the numbers, the decision that followed, and the reason if the council decided otherwise.

goals.title: We take in what people bring us between rounds
goals.description: What residents report unprompted – the report, the idea, the complaint – we invite rather than wait for; we answer it within a deadline, count it when many people say the same thing, and use it to decide what we ask next.

goals.title: The back office stays available, and switched off
goals.description: Fees, permits, spending by neighbourhood and the assets maintained by the service company are here so that the local government can see them working and switch them on if it decides to. It is deliberately the second act.

objectives.title: We build the register of people and things within the town boundary and let people correct their own record
objectives.description: People, households, businesses and informal traders, and the properties and parcel numbers where they live, trade from and pay for – each tied to a neighbourhood, built from what the local government already holds rather than from a census, and corrected by the people in it, with its source shown on every record. One register, not twelve spreadsheets kept by department.

objectives.title: We report which neighbourhoods the register barely covers
objectives.description: The register is a claim about who exists, and the places with gaps are exactly the ones a consultation gets wrong. It is met when the coverage of every neighbourhood is published before the round opens, and the gaps are named rather than discovered after a round that went badly.

objectives.title: We keep contact details and consent together
objectives.description: Knowing how to reach someone is only useful if the contact is lawful and provable. It is met when the consent given can be produced as it stood on the day it was given, and a withdrawal is carried out on the same working day it arrives.

objectives.title: We start a round with its method written down in advance
objectives.description: Every round carries its question, audience, period, channels and the way the answers will be read – fixed before it opens, so that the method cannot be fitted to the result afterwards. It is met when the round runs for at least four weeks, or records why a shorter period was proportionate to what it asks.

objectives.title: We reach those who never answer online
objectives.description: Older residents, people without data plans, people who do not trust the local government and people who simply do not read notices – reached on paper, at markets and at the gate, and counted just like everyone else. It is met when every round names at least one device-free channel and reports separately what it brought in.

objectives.title: We count each person once and publish the denominator
objectives.description: One voice per person, duplicates discarded with a reason, and every result stated as a number out of a number, so that nobody has to guess whether forty responses are a mandate. The response rate a neighbourhood must reach is the local government's own threshold, named before the round opens and published with the result.

objectives.title: We record answers as records, readable by neighbourhood and by topic
objectives.description: The responses belong in the local government's own register, where they can be queried across rounds and neighbourhoods, not in the form that happened to collect them.

objectives.title: We publish the result with everything needed to judge it
objectives.description: The question asked, the period, the channels, how many out of how many responded, the breakdown by neighbourhood, and the free text summarised, without polish.

objectives.title: We write the decision into the round's report
objectives.description: The local government's decision on a round goes into the round's own report, together with the reasoning if it went against the weight of the opinions heard. There is no separate decision register.

objectives.title: We tell the report's groups what happened
objectives.description: The result reaches the groups to which the round's report is published, like any report. Someone who responded through a public link and is in none of the groups is not notified. There is no deadline for it, but a consultation that never reports back teaches people not to respond next time.

objectives.title: We take reports from anyone, on any channel, without an account
objectives.description: At the service desk, by phone, online, at a meeting, at a market stall or through a council member – in every case the same record. The resident submits it themselves, the council member on their behalf, or the field helper records it, with the name of the person who took it shown.

objectives.title: We ask for reports between rounds instead of waiting for them
objectives.description: A local government that hears only from those who seek it out keeps hearing the same few. It is met when every neighbourhood is asked at set intervals what it would like to raise – through the channels its residents actually use, including a device-free one.

objectives.title: We confirm, give a case number, and keep it visible while it is open
objectives.description: Whoever made a report gets a case number within five working days and an answer within ten working days; everyone else can see what has been reported, what is being looked into and what has been decided, rejections included. Anything past its deadline is on the list of overdue items, which the council sees at every meeting.

objectives.title: We count how many raised the same thing and name the neighbourhoods that raised nothing
objectives.description: Forty people reporting the same thing is the number that makes the board politically useful, so merging duplicates keeps every reporter rather than discarding them. And silence is information too: the neighbourhoods that reported nothing this quarter are published beside the board, for the same reason a round publishes its coverage.

objectives.title: We hand over operations matters and track what came back
objectives.description: Most of what residents report is the work of the company to which the local government has outsourced its services. The council's job is to pass it on, to know what happened, and to be able to say so in public.

objectives.title: We let what people keep raising decide what we ask next
objectives.description: The board is the cheapest agenda a local government will ever get. It is met when a round's question can name the reports it comes from, and the topics most often reported in the quarter are put in front of whoever decides what the next round asks.

objectives.title: We publish the schedule of fees and charges
objectives.description: The lightest and politically heaviest part of back-office operations: what the local government charges, published in the version in force before it is applied.

objectives.title: We handle applications and permits when the council switches it on
objectives.description: Application, inspection, a decision with a stated reason, fee and renewal – it is built in and can be demonstrated, waiting for a council that wants the closed loop.

objectives.title: We show how much we spent by neighbourhood when the council switches it on
objectives.description: Budget against actuals by neighbourhood and by service, which is the answer every public hearing ends with. The budget by neighbourhood and by service is kept as its own set of accounts, so what was voted and what was spent are the same kind of record and can be read side by side.

objectives.title: We record who may approve what, and up to what amount
objectives.description: Which role may authorise a payment, permit or contract, and the limit above which someone else must be approached. Written against the role, not carried in someone's head, so that an approval can later be checked against the limit in force that day.

objectives.title: We build the upward report from the same figures we published
objectives.description: Council reports, budget against actuals by department and by neighbourhood, and the reports requested by the national level – from the same records the local government published locally, so that the figure given to a resident and the figure sent upward cannot differ.

objectives.title: Every year we tell residents what we asked, what we heard and what changed
objectives.description: The annual report is built from the records of rounds and decisions, broken down by neighbourhood, with the name of the person responsible; it goes public only after a person approves it.

objectives.title: We publish the fee schedule in the version that is in force today
objectives.description: The fee and charges schedule always shows the version in force, with its effective date and the preceding version preserved, so that the council and the resident can refer to the same dated schedule.

objectives.title: We carry the permit from application to decision and expiry date along one traceable path
objectives.description: The application, the inspector's finding, the decision and the renewal due at expiry stay in a single case, so the applicant can always see where it stands and what the inspector found stands behind the decision.

objectives.title: The call for civil-society grants and the assessment criteria are known in advance, in public
objectives.description: Before every call is published, we fix the budget, the deadline and the criteria, so that the applicant and the resident see the same thing as the assessor.

objectives.title: Awarding the grant and the final report can be followed in the same register
objectives.description: The amount awarded, the beneficiary and the status of the report are in one place, so behind every payment there is always a person's signature and an accountable statement of expenses.

objectives.title: We get the notice to the right neighbourhoods and count who acknowledged it
objectives.description: An official notice or alert goes out only after approval, to the neighbourhoods it affects, through at least one device-free channel, and until it is closed we publish, by neighbourhood, how many of those sent it have acknowledged it.

objectives.title: We answer risk questions from the register, not from guesswork
objectives.description: The chat answers the five simple questions and the biggest gaps from live data; if a name fits two risks or controls, it offers choice buttons, and it makes nothing up.

objectives.title: Every conflict-of-interest declaration is on record and nobody exceeds their approval limit
objectives.description: The declarations of council members and approving roles are in one place, the approval limit is written against the role, and the system does not allow an amount above the limit to be approved but routes it to another role.

objectives.title: Every new hazard enters the register with an owner and controls
objectives.description: A department head enters the new risk with causes, consequences and controls; the AI only produces a draft, a person approves it before saving, and the register rejects an unknown owner.

objectives.title: Every control shows whether it works or has stopped working
objectives.description: The department head attaches evidence to a control and sees its status change from unproven to proven; failed or outdated evidence resets the status, and the outdating shows up as a gap on the gap list. The AI only summarises and counts; a person approves the assessment.

objectives.title: Every gap becomes a task with an owner and a deadline on the council board, and we see when it closes
objectives.description: From a gap in a control, the department head starts an action, which becomes an ordinary task on the council's board with an owner and a deadline; the AI only drafts a suggestion, a person approves the creation, and the gap comes off the list when the task is done and the control has been assessed.

objectives.title: The council meeting pack carries the risks: failing controls, serious gaps and overdue actions, each with an owner
objectives.description: On the day of the meeting the town clerk has the risk part of the meeting pack compiled from the register; the AI only collects, counts and drafts, and a person approves what goes into the pack and in front of the public.

values.text: A consultation that hears only the loud misleads the council more than no consultation at all, because it arrives with the authority of a number.
We say what changed because people spoke up – and also when nothing did, and why. The second kind of answer is what makes the first believable.
We publish a number, not a person. Everything this agency collects is given with some degree of trust, and that trust is the asset.
The council asks only what it is willing to act on, or says plainly that it is asking in order to learn. A question whose answer changes nothing teaches people that answering is pointless.
Nobody should need a smartphone to be heard. The residents hardest to reach online often have the most at stake in the decision.
The register is a claim about who exists. The council is at least as accountable for those who are missing from it as for those who are in it.
What someone brings unasked is worth more than what they say when asked, because they chose the topic. A council that only gets answers to its own questions never learns what it forgot to ask.

What the local government charges, and what it spent in a neighbourhood, is public before anyone has to ask. Back-office operations are dark in this template because the council did not ask for them, not because the numbers are anyone's secret.

The number the resident gets and the number sent to the national level are the same number. A local government that reports one number upward and another downward keeps two sets of books, whatever it calls them.

rules.text: Closes by publishing the round's coverage: by neighbourhood, how many responded out of those the register holds there, naming every neighbourhood below the round's own minimum.
A response counts once per person. A duplicate is discarded with a reason, and the number of discards is published with the result.
The published result carries the question asked, the period, the channels used, and how many responded out of those who could have.

Identifiable responses may be read only by the Data and analysis officer and the Data protection and records officer, only within the round in which they were given, and only against a recorded purpose.
A decision against the weight of the opinions heard writes its reason into the round's own report, the same report that carries the result.
No round runs on digital channels alone. Every round names at least one device-free channel and reports what it brought in.
We acknowledge a report within five working days and answer it within ten working days. Anything that exceeds the deadline is on the list of overdue items, which the council sees at every meeting.
The board publishes its own numbers: how many people reported each thing, and which neighbourhoods reported nothing this quarter.
The register's coverage is published by neighbourhood before the round opens, and no neighbourhood counts as consulted where the register is below the council's own threshold.
A report made on someone's behalf names who made it and who it comes from, and the person it comes from is notified that it was reported.
A fee is charged only after its schedule has been published in the version in force.
We do not approve a payment, permit or contract above the limit set for the approving role, and we check against the limit in force that day.
An AI role only drafts, summarises, looks things up or counts; anything that goes before the public is approved by a person first.
The owner of a risk is the head of the department of the service the risk affects; they see only the risks of their own service.
The council and the mayor's office read the whole risk register.

workflows.name: Keeping the register up to date
workflows.description: How the register of people, households and businesses is built, how the people in it can correct their own data, and how we report where coverage is thin.

workflows.name: A consultation round from start to finish
workflows.description: From the moment the town council decides to ask its residents, through the questionnaire, the channels and the answering period, to the received, counted and published result.

workflows.name: What residents bring us
workflows.description: From the moment a report arrives on any channel – the resident makes it themselves, a council member records it on their behalf, or the liaison team working in the field takes it – through the confirmation and the public output, to counting how many people reported the same thing, all the way to the next round's question. The AI roles may only draft, summarise, follow up and count; anything that goes before the public is always approved by a person.

workflows.name: From result through decision to feedback
workflows.description: How the published result becomes a council proposal, a recorded decision, and a message to those who answered.

workflows.name: The administration back office
workflows.description: The back office of case handling, which the town council can switch on later: what it bills, applications and permits from start to finish, the budget and the actual expenditure by neighbourhood, who may approve what and up to what amount, and the report sent upward.

workflows.name: The monthly invitation to one neighbourhood
workflows.description: How the town council asks every neighbourhood each month what it would like put on the agenda: from totalling what has come in, through the posted notice and the personal approaches, to counting the answers. The AI roles may only draft, summarise, follow up and count (RU-AI-1); anything that goes before the public is always approved by a person.

workflows.name: Checking a promise when it falls due
workflows.description: When the deadline of a promise made by the council expires, we check whether it was kept, and publish what we heard from residents and what it changed: every promise is marked kept, partly kept or not kept.

workflows.name: Request to see, receive or delete one's own data
workflows.description: From the moment a Zöldhalom resident wants to view, obtain or have deleted the data the town council holds on them, through identification, gathering the data and the decision, to the dated reply and the note of what happened.

workflows.name: Reviewing a decision afterwards
workflows.description: How the audit committee examines a decision already made: what we heard before the decision, what it changed in it, what the council replied, and how this reaches those who answered. The AI roles may only draft, summarise, follow up and count; anything that goes before the public is always approved by a person.

workflows.name: Reaching the thinly covered neighbourhoods
workflows.description: How we reach the neighbourhoods where the register is thin: we show where it is incomplete, form an outreach team for each neighbourhood, write a call, seek out those who have not answered, and then recount the coverage.

workflows.name: Handing an operations report to the service contractor
workflows.description: From the moment the residents' reports made between rounds come together into an operational case, through the handover and the service company's feedback, until the opened piece of work is closed against the original report.

workflows.name: Merging identical reports and counting those who raised them
workflows.description: How we merge the reports residents bring unprompted about the same thing into a single topic, and how we count, once per person, how many stand behind it.

workflows.name: A quick vote on a single question
workflows.description: A short round started by the Consultation lead that puts a single question to all four neighbourhoods of Zöldhalom (Óváros, Kertváros, Malomsor, Határrét) and closes with a short, dated result. The aim is that the whole neighbourhood speaks, not the loudest.

workflows.name: Residents' forum or neighbourhood meeting
workflows.description: From convening the forum, through the invitation, counting attendance and the minutes, until the neighbourhood learns what we heard from it and what will come of it.

workflows.name: A council member's neighbourhood surgery hour
workflows.description: From the moment the council member announces their consultation hour in their neighbourhood, through recording what was said in person as a report, to the feedback: we ask the whole neighbourhood, not the loudest.

workflows.name: The list of late matters at every council meeting
workflows.description: For every meeting we collect the reports past their promised deadline by neighbourhood, with a named person responsible, and publish them after approval.

workflows.name: Finding and merging duplicate records
workflows.description: How we find and merge duplicate records of people, households, businesses and properties so that each person, household, business and property has a single record. The AI roles may only draft, summarise, follow up and count; the merge and anything that goes before the public is always approved by a person.

workflows.name: Council meeting: agenda, proposals, minutes
workflows.description: How the material for a Zöldhalom council meeting is prepared, from the agenda to the minutes and the register of resolutions, so that nobody can quietly rewrite what was said and what was changed.

workflows.name: Moderating a report without silencing anyone
workflows.description: How the community moderator handles what people bring between rounds: publishing, holding back or rejecting a report, with the reason recorded, so that criticism of the town council never disappears.

workflows.name: Reviewing the questionnaire before we send it out
workflows.description: From the moment the questions of the Zöldhalom round have been written, until the revised question set and a paper sheet carrying the same questions can be sent out: in Óváros, Kertváros, Malomsor and Határrét as well. The AI roles may only draft, summarise, follow up and count; anything that goes before the public is always approved by a person.

workflows.name: Choosing what the council asks
workflows.description: From the moment the mayor decides to start a new round, until the council publishes a single question it can stand behind, built from the council members' proposals and from what residents signalled in the neighbourhoods.

workflows.name: When the decision goes against what we heard
workflows.description: How we say publicly what we heard from residents, where the council decided differently, what the reason is, and who carries the matter on.

workflows.name: Public-interest data request
workflows.description: How the town council answers a request for public-interest data: registration, finding the requested documents, marking the parts that cannot be released, then a reply within the legal deadline, or a reasoned refusal. The AI roles may only draft, summarise, follow up and count; anything that goes before the public is always approved by a person.

workflows.name: The annual report to residents
workflows.description: Every year we tell residents what we asked, what we heard, and what changed because of it: with numbers, by neighbourhood, with the name of the person responsible.

workflows.name: Back-office operation: always at hand, switched on only by council decision
workflows.description: How we keep the back office (accounting, task management, digital twin) on standby, and how the council switches on the second phase whenever it wants. The AI roles may only draft, summarise, follow up and count; anything that goes before the public is always approved by a person.

workflows.name: Publishing the fee schedule in the version in force
workflows.description: How the Zöldhalom town council's schedule of fees and charges gets from the finance officer to the noticeboard and the page, so that the version in force, with its date, is always the one shown, and the earlier one is kept.

workflows.name: A permit from application to decision
workflows.description: How an application for a Zöldhalom building or use permit travels from acceptance, through the inspector's finding and the decision, to the renewal day, so that the fee, the finding and the decision stay in the same case.

workflows.name: The upward report from the published figures
workflows.description: How the financial report sent to the national level is prepared from the same ledger and the same results that the town council published locally, so that the number shown to residents and the number sent upward cannot differ.

workflows.name: Grants to civil organisations: call, application, decision, final report
workflows.description: How the Zöldhalom town council announces, assesses and monitors a civil society grant framework so that the public sees the call, the decision and the report from the same register, and the payment of the money bears a person's signature.

workflows.name: A notice or alert: to the right neighbourhoods, on the right channels, with acknowledgement
workflows.description: How an official Zöldhalom announcement or emergency alert reaches the right neighbourhoods on the right channels so that a person approves it first, and afterwards we count who acknowledged it.

workflows.name: Booking a hall, room or event slot
workflows.description: How a Zöldhalom association or resident requests, receives and confirms a room, premises or event slot: without a clash, at the fee in the published fee schedule, and so that the town clerk approves the booking.

workflows.name: Setting and collecting a fee and tracking those in arrears
workflows.description: How the finance officer of the Zöldhalom town council sets a charge (for example a waste collection fee or a public space use fee), how each payer gets a separate receivable, how the payment arrives, and how the list of overdue debts by age is prepared, so that the arrears age from the day of assessment and the reminder is approved by the town clerk.

workflows.name: Budget and spending by neighbourhood
workflows.description: How the Zöldhalom town council's budget milestone, performance certification and retained amount get from the finance officer to the residents, so that it shows by neighbourhood how large the allocation is and how much we have spent, and the statement is approved by the town clerk.

workflows.name: A question to the chat assistant about risks
workflows.description: How a department head or the council gets an answer to a risk question in the chat: the question, the search in the register, the choice buttons when names match, the biggest gaps by owner, then the owner's check. The AI role may only draft, summarise, follow up and count; anything that is made public is always approved by a person.

workflows.name: Conflict-of-interest declarations and approval limits
workflows.description: How a council member's conflict of interest declaration is entered in the register, and how approval stays within the limit set for the role: the declaration, entry in the register, assessing the involvement and setting the limit, checking the amount against the limit, supplying missing declarations, then the mayor's approval. The system stops any amount above the limit. The AI role may only draft, summarise, follow up and count; anything that is made public is always approved by a person.

workflows.name: Adding a new risk and its controls
workflows.description: How a new risk gets into the register: the department head describes the hazard and names the owner, the assistant gives a draft of the causes, consequences and controls, the department head approves it, the town clerk checks the owner (if the owner is unknown, the entry is rejected), then the risk is saved, and the council reader sees it in the register. The AI role may only draft; what it saves is first approved by a person.

workflows.name: Attaching evidence and tracking a control's status
workflows.description: How the status of a control changes under the effect of evidence: the department head attaches a report to the control, the assistant summarises the report and gives a suggestion for the result, the department head approves it and records the evidence, the assistant counts the controls by status (proven, weak, unproven, failed), the council reader sees the new status, and the department head reviews the gaps caused by outdated evidence. Going out of date appears only as a gap; no message goes to anyone, and no task is created by itself. The AI role may only draft and count; what is recorded is approved by a person.

workflows.name: A gap becomes a task on the council board, and closes
workflows.description: How a gap becomes a task: the department head looks at their own gaps, the assistant gives a suggestion for the action and the deadline, the department head approves it and creates the action, which becomes an ordinary task on the council's board with an owner and a deadline, the owner completes it on the board, the department head closes the action and assesses the control, and the town clerk sees at the council meeting, on the list of overdue tasks, that it has closed. The AI role may only draft and count; creating the task is always approved by a person.

workflows.name: The council meeting pack shows the risks
workflows.description: How the risks get before the council: the town clerk asks for the risk section on the day of the meeting, the assistant collects from the register the faulty controls, the serious gaps and the overdue actions with their owners and drafts a text, the department heads correct their own rows, the council risk reader reviews it for clarity, the town clerk approves it and attaches it to the meeting material, and the mayor goes through it at the meeting. The AI role may only collect, count and draft; what goes into the package and before the public is always approved by a person.

workflows.name: We assign an address to the neighbourhood
workflows.description: How every record lands in the right neighbourhood's count: the data and analysis officer collects the addresses without a neighbourhood, finds the neighbourhood from their location, flags where the entered and the calculated neighbourhood differ, or the point is inside neither boundary, a person makes the decision, and the records are counted by neighbourhood. The AI role may only collect, count and draft; what goes before the public is first approved by a person.

workflows.name: A sensitive or anonymous report
workflows.description: How we handle what residents bring between rounds when it is sensitive or anonymous: the report arrives without identity, the sender gets an anonymous receipt code, the data protection and records officer judges the sensitivity, a person removes the identifying details, the case goes to the right department, and before publication the small-numbers rule decides. The AI role may only draft, summarise and count; what goes before the public is always approved by a person.

workflows.name: A resident registering or correcting their own record
workflows.description: How a resident can register or correct their own record: the form opens only if every question on it has a field in the register, the answer goes to the module that holds the data, the source, the contact and the consent stay together as the resident's, and a person approves corrections to identifying data. The AI roles may only draft, summarise, follow up and count; anything that goes before the public is always approved by a person.

workflows.name: Giving and withdrawing consent
workflows.description: How the town council asks for and keeps consent: the numbered versions of the consent text, who accepted which version and when, and the withdrawal, which must be carried out the same day: that person's answers and messages are hidden, but not deleted. The AI roles may only draft, summarise, follow up and count; anything that goes before the public is always approved by a person.

workflows.name: A round on paper, by phone or in person
workflows.description: How the round's question reaches those who have no smartphone: we choose the way of reaching them household by household, a paper sheet, a phone script and an in-person conversation are prepared with the same questions, a clerk records the returned sheets on the round's own form with the "in whose name" field and a paper marker, and in the count everyone counts once in the same way. The AI role only drafts, counts and reminds; what goes before the public is approved by a person.

workflows.name: We count each person once and publish the coverage
workflows.description: How the town council counts a round's answers once per person: the denominator from the register, filtering out the repeated answer from the same verified contact, merging or leaving out groups that are too small, then publishing the coverage together with who did not answer and what we left out. The AI roles may only draft, count, summarise and remind; anything that goes before the public is always approved by a person.

workflows.name: Participatory budget vote
workflows.description: How we ask the whole neighbourhood, not the loudest, what the council should spend money on: the Finance officer assigns an amount to the neighbourhood, residents propose, the town clerk reviews the proposals from a budget and legal point of view, everyone may vote once per person, and the council decides from the ranking. The AI roles may only draft, summarise, follow up and count; anything that goes before the public is always approved by a person.

work_items.title: Let us build the register from what the town council already holds
work_items.description: Let us build the first version from the lists we already have, not from a census.
work_items.prompt: Work from what Zöldhalom Town Council already has: the electoral roll, the property or parcel number list, the business and market registers, and each department's mailing lists. Load properties as records in their own right, not as an address typed against a person, because the fee, the household and the business all end up pointing to the property. Assign every record to a neighbourhood (Óváros, Kertváros, Malomsor or Határrét), and note which source it came from, because a record of unknown origin can later be neither corrected nor defended. Do not merge two sources into one person unless something genuinely identifies them as the same person; a duplicate is easier to live with than a wrongly merged record. The AI role may only summarise, count and word a merge suggestion; a person approves the merge and any public statement.
work_items.form_name: Let us build the register from what the town council already holds

work_items.title: Let us let everyone correct their own record
work_items.description: Let us give residents the chance to correct what the local government holds about them.
work_items.prompt: Let us show residents what the register holds about them – their neighbourhood, their contact details, how they would like to be contacted – and let them correct it without an account and without giving a reason. Note that the change came from the person, not from the office. Only a register that the public can correct stays true. The AI role may at most word a reminder or count the corrections received; a person approves the rewriting of the record.
work_items.form_name: Let us let everyone correct their own record

work_items.title: Let us report where the register is thin
work_items.description: Let us publish the coverage of the register itself, by neighbourhood.
work_items.prompt: For every neighbourhood, report how many people the system has on record compared with the best outside estimate of those living there, and for how many of those records there is a usable contact. Every quarter, name the three thinnest neighbourhoods. The liaison work (O-5) must be done in these before the next round, not after. The AI role may count the figures and summarise them in text; a person approves publication.
work_items.form_name: Let us report where the register is thin

work_items.title: Let us record consent as a version, not as a tick
work_items.description: Let us record what someone agreed to, in the words they saw.
work_items.prompt: Note which consent text, in which language and in which version the person saw when they agreed, and what it covered: a consultation approach, reading an identified answer, appearing in a published quotation. Keep the text itself, not a reference to the “privacy notice”, because the notice will change, and the question of what they agreed to will be asked on the day they agreed.
work_items.form_name: Let us record consent as a version, not as a tick

work_items.title: Let us carry out the withdrawal the same day
work_items.description: Let us make stopping easy, and prove that it stopped.
work_items.prompt: Accept a withdrawal through any channel, including one said aloud to a council member, and apply it on the same day across every channel. Note when it arrived and when it took effect. Confirm it back to the person. A town council that is slow to stop contacting someone has already lost the argument about whether that person's opinion can be entrusted to it.
work_items.form_name: Let us carry out the withdrawal the same day

work_items.title: Let us frame the question the town council is truly willing to act on
work_items.description: We turn the political intent into a question worth asking.
work_items.prompt: The question is written so that every answer leads in a direction the town council can really set off in. In the round's own documentation they record what the town council will do with each of the likely outcomes, and if the decision is already limited by law, money or a contract, they say so in the question itself. If the honest answer is that the town council wants to learn rather than commit, they write that down and publish it together with the question.
work_items.form_name: Let us frame the question the town council is truly willing to act on

work_items.title: We put the procedure in writing before the round opens
work_items.description: We record how we will read the answers while we still do not know them.
work_items.prompt: They record the target audience, the period, the channels, the lowest reach the round aims for, the way free text is sorted into topics, and the way the result will be communicated. Before the round opens, the Audit committee chair should see it too. This document is what distinguishes a consultation from a search for agreement.
work_items.form_name: We put the procedure in writing before the round opens

work_items.title: We have the questionnaire reviewed before we send it out
work_items.description: We check that the round does not ask for more than is needed.
work_items.prompt: The Data protection and records officer measures the questionnaire against the round's purpose: every identifying question must earn its place, and whatever would tie the answers of a small neighbourhood to a single household must be coarsened or dropped. They record the review and the changes made as a result.
work_items.form_name: We have the questionnaire reviewed before we send it out

work_items.title: We designate the channels, including one that needs no device
work_items.description: We plan the outreach before the question is even sent out.
work_items.prompt: They list every channel the round will use and whom it intends to reach. At least one must be usable without a smartphone and without knowing the official language: paper at the market, a table at a residents' forum, knocking on gates, a telephone line. They name the owner of each channel and how many people they expect to reach with it.
work_items.form_name: We designate the channels, including one that needs no device

work_items.title: We collect in person, and bring everything back in full
work_items.description: We run the paper half of the round and bring it into the same register as the rest.
work_items.prompt: On paper or in conversation, they collect with the same questions, in the same order, as on the online questionnaire. They record where, when and by whom each batch was collected. The batch is entered within the round's period, never after its close, and the paper is kept until the end of the round's retention period. A late-entered answer is an answer that silently did not count.
work_items.form_name: We collect in person, and bring everything back in full

work_items.title: We count once per person, and record what we left out
work_items.description: We make the counting defensible before we publish it.
work_items.prompt: Where possible they match the answers to the register, and drop duplicates while recording the reason. The number of skipped answers is reported alongside the result. Where an answer cannot be matched to anyone in the register, they count those too and say how many there were: an answer that cannot be matched is a resident the register does not know, which is a finding for goal O-2, not a reason to throw away what they said.
work_items.form_name: We count once per person, and record what we left out

work_items.title: We load the answers into the register
work_items.description: We take the responses out of the questionnaire and put them into a register that outlives it.
work_items.prompt: Every response is to be entered into the council's own register, tied to the round, the neighbourhood, and either one person or an explicit anonymous marker. Free text is to be sorted into themes, and the original words are kept next to the theme. Before anyone publishes a number, compare the count loaded with the count collected, and list whatever cannot be loaded instead of quietly dropping it. The AI role (RU-AI-1) may only draft, summarise, remind or count; anything that goes before the public is always approved by a person.
work_items.form_name: We load the answers into the register

work_items.title: We publish the coverage, by neighbourhood
work_items.description: In the same breath as the result, we say whom we heard and whom we did not.
work_items.prompt: For each neighbourhood, report how many of those in the register responded, and flag every neighbourhood that fell below the round's own minimum. State plainly where the result is not representative. A round that ends with four neighbourhoods unheard is still useful, as long as no one reading it believes it speaks for those four, for example Óváros, Kertváros, Malomsor or Határrét. The AI role (RU-AI-1) may only draft, summarise, remind or count; anything that goes before the public is always approved by a person.
work_items.form_name: We publish the coverage, by neighbourhood

work_items.title: Let us take a report through any channel, from the resident or on their behalf
work_items.description: Let us record what someone brought, without making them work for it, and name who took it.
work_items.prompt: We accept it in whatever form it arrives: typed into the public form, read out over the phone at the cash desk, written on a sheet of paper at the market stall, or handed to a council member at a meeting. We ask only four things: what, where, in which neighbourhood, and how the person can be reached – the last one may be declined. Where a photo helps, we take it; a picture of a collapsed drain settles an argument that a paragraph does not. If someone else records it on their behalf, we name that person on the record, and also the person the report comes from, then notify them that it has been recorded, under the same identifier. Never ask for an account before hearing the resident. The AI role (RU-AI-1) may only summarise an incoming report and draft a suggested classification; a person approves it.
work_items.form_name: Let us take a report through any channel, from the resident or on their behalf

work_items.title: Let us ask the neighbourhood what it would like put on the agenda
work_items.description: Let us go out and ask at a set pace, not wait at the service desk.
work_items.prompt: We choose a rhythm the council can keep – monthly is easier to keep than weekly – and we do keep it, because a call that comes twice and then stops is worse than none. It is published as a standing notice for each neighbourhood separately, not for the whole town, so that the response can be attributed from the start; residents reply in the notice's thread, in their neighbourhood's room. We use the channel that the residents of that neighbourhood actually use, and one of them must be a channel that needs no device: a notice at the market, a word at the house of worship, a sheet that the liaison team takes with them. We say clearly what the council can and cannot do, and we say what became of the previous batch – people answer a call that follows a visible result, and not one that follows silence. The AI role (RU-AI-1) may only draft the call and prepare it for sending, then count the responses; a person approves the sending.
work_items.form_name: Let us ask the neighbourhood what it would like put on the agenda

work_items.title: Let us confirm back within the deadline
work_items.description: Let us give the person an identifier and a date within five working days.
work_items.prompt: The acknowledgement is not the answer, and it must not look like one: it says that we have it, this is its identifier, this person is handling it, and this is when it will get a reply. We send it on the channel it came in on. Where the person making the report gave no contact details, the identifier still exists and opens the case from the public board, so that even someone who gave nothing can follow it. At the same moment we start the ten-working-day clock for the substantive reply, and let it run in public. The AI role (RU-AI-1) may prepare the text of the acknowledgement and watch the deadlines; a person approves the sending.
work_items.form_name: Let us confirm back within the deadline

work_items.title: Let us moderate without silencing
work_items.description: Let us keep the board usable, and leave the criticism on it.
work_items.prompt: We remove abuse, personal attacks and anything that identifies a private individual. We merge duplicates, and say so publicly. Criticism of the council, its decisions and its officials stays where it is. Every removal is recorded with its reason, and whoever posted it can see the reason. The AI role (RU-AI-1) may only flag and draft a proposal; a person approves the removal.
work_items.form_name: Let us moderate without silencing

work_items.title: Let us route it, and keep it visible
work_items.description: Let us assign an owner, and let the public see how it is progressing.
work_items.prompt: We assign each item to the council member or official who will answer it, and set the date by which they will answer. We show the public what state it is in. Where the answer is no, we publish the no together with its reason – nobody believes a board of open items on which nothing is ever turned down. The AI role (RU-AI-1) may only remind and follow up on deadlines; a person approves a refusal and its publication.
work_items.form_name: Let us route it, and keep it visible

work_items.title: Let us count how many reported the same thing
work_items.description: Let us merge duplicates so that we do not lose a single reporter.
work_items.prompt: Two hundred reports about a single junction is the strongest political fact the board will ever produce, and it is destroyed the moment merging loses the second reporter. So we merge the item, never the people: every reporter stays attached, keeps their own identifier, and is notified of the outcome individually. We publish the number on the board – “43 people reported it” is what moves an item up the agenda. If a merge is wrong, it must be reversible, because a wrongly merged complaint looks to the person who made it like a buried complaint. The AI role (RU-AI-1) may draft a merge proposal and count; a person approves the merge.
work_items.form_name: Let us count how many reported the same thing

work_items.title: Let us report the neighbourhoods that report nothing
work_items.description: Let us publish the silence beside the board, the way a round publishes its coverage.
work_items.prompt: A neighbourhood that reports nothing is either satisfied or not being reached, and the two look identical in a single number. Every quarter we publish the number for each neighbourhood and let that neighbourhood's council member account for it – that is the conversation the number is meant to start. We do not treat silence as approval in any document that goes before the council. Where a neighbourhood is consistently silent, the next round's no-device channel must go there first. The AI role (RU-AI-1) may only count and summarise; a person approves the publication.
work_items.form_name: Let us report the neighbourhoods that report nothing

work_items.title: Let us hand the operational matters over to the service contractor
work_items.description: Let us pass on what is not the local government's own work, and keep hold of the thread.
work_items.prompt: We send the item to the service contractor with the location and the content as reported, and record the identifier we get back from them. The council keeps its own record open until completion is reported. The resident asked the council, so the council answers, not the contractor. The AI role (RU-AI-1) may only draft a summary for the handover and follow up on completion; a person approves the handover.
work_items.form_name: Let us hand the operational matters over to the service contractor

work_items.title: Let us review publicly what came back
work_items.description: Let us make the outsourced party visible to those who pay for it.
work_items.prompt: Every month we report how many items went to the service contractor, how many came back done, and in how long. We publish it. Where the contractor's own data and the residents' reports differ, we say so rather than quietly reconciling them – the council's leverage over an outsourced service is largely this report. The AI role (RU-AI-1) may count and summarise the monthly data in text; a person approves the publication.
work_items.form_name: Let us review publicly what came back

work_items.title: Let us carry the regularly recurring topics into the next round's question
work_items.description: Let us shape the quarter's most frequent topics into the next question.
work_items.prompt: Every quarter we put the ten most frequently reported topics before whoever puts the consultation programme together, with the numbers and the neighbourhoods they came from. Most will not become a round, and that is fine – what matters is that someone decided, in front of the evidence, not to ask, rather than no one. Where a topic becomes a round, we name on the round itself the reports it came from, so that those who reported can see that their report became the question. The AI role (RU-AI-1) may only summarise and count; a person approves the compilation of the programme.
work_items.form_name: Let us carry the regularly recurring topics into the next round's question

work_items.title: We publish the result in full
work_items.description: We put the finding where anyone can check it.
work_items.prompt: Publish the question exactly as it was asked, the period, the channels, the numbers with the denominator and the skipped answers, the breakdown by neighbourhood, and the themes with typical quotes that identify no one. Publish the procedure description alongside it. The result must be published even when it is uncomfortable, and especially then. The AI role (RU-AI-1) may only draft, summarise, remind or count; anything that goes before the public is always approved by a person.

work_items.title: We take the result to the council as a proposal
work_items.description: We turn the finding into a decision that someone has to take.
work_items.prompt: The proposal contains the result, the council's real options, and what each one costs. Attach the procedure description and the coverage numbers, so that the council member can see how much weight the finding carries. Name the role responsible for the decision. The AI role (RU-AI-1) may only draft, summarise, remind or count; anything that goes before the public is always approved by a person.

work_items.title: We enter the decision in the report
work_items.description: The decision lives in the round's report, not in a separate register and not only in the minutes.
work_items.prompt: Enter in the round report what was decided, by whom, and on which day. If the decision goes against the weight of what most of those heard said, write the reason in the report too: money, law, contract, a longer-term plan, or a judgement that the council takes responsibility for. No separate decision register needs to be kept. The AI role (RU-AI-1) may prepare the text of the entry only as a draft; the decision and the reason entered in the report are always approved by a person.

work_items.title: We notify the report's groups
work_items.description: The groups on the report learn of the result as they would of any report.
work_items.prompt: Publish the report to the groups the round was addressed to, so that they learn the result the way they learn of any report. Whoever responded through a public link and is in none of the groups is not notified. Say what was decided and what happens next, and if nothing happens yet, say that too. Keep it short enough to be read on a phone and simple enough to be read aloud. The AI role (RU-AI-1) may only draft, summarise, remind or count; anything that goes before the public is always approved by a person.

work_items.title: We record the outcome of the promises when the deadline passes
work_items.description: Every promise in the report is a task with a deadline; its outcome is approved by a person.
work_items.prompt: At publication, list every promise in the report, each with a deadline; each becomes a task. When a task's deadline passes, record its outcome: fulfilled, partly fulfilled or not fulfilled. The outcome is shown beside the report to everyone who can read the report. The AI role (RU-AI-1) may only count the reminders and deadlines and send reminders; a person approves the outcome before it becomes visible beside the report.

work_items.title: We publish the fee schedule in its valid version
work_items.description: We keep what the local government bills public and dated.
work_items.prompt: Publish the schedule of fees and charges before it is applied, keep every year's version, and make it possible to look up the version in force on any past day. This is the easiest administrative item, and the one most likely to be asked about at a council meeting, for example the rents in forints (Ft). The AI role may only draft, summarise, remind or count; anything that goes before the public is always approved by a person.

work_items.title: We guide one application through to the decision
work_items.description: We show the closed loop that the local government has not yet asked for.
work_items.prompt: Take one real application all the way through the schedule: recorded on arrival with a date, screened, a site visit with a result for each line, the reason for the decision marked, the fee set, the permit issued with its expiry. This shows what the closed round gives, and let us be honest: it only pays off if the council is ready to run it.

work_items.title: We show the expenditure by neighbourhood
work_items.description: We answer the question that every public meeting comes down to.
work_items.prompt: Show the budget and the actual spending by neighbourhood and by service, including how much was paid to the service company. Where the council lacks the data needed for this, show the skeleton and say exactly what has to be fed in: an honest gap is worth more than a filled-in example that no one can reproduce. The AI role may only draft, summarise, remind or count; anything that goes before the public is always approved by a person.

work_items.title: We write down who may approve what, and up to what amount
work_items.description: We write the authority against the role, with its limit, before anyone needs it.
work_items.prompt: Take the council's existing scheme of delegation and attach every line to a role, not to a person: what this role may authorise, up to what amount at most (Ft), and who gets the case above that. Record the day each limit took effect and keep the old ones, because an approval is measured against the limit in force that day, not today's. Where the council never wrote this down, which is common, say so plainly instead of inventing an amount, and put the gap before the council as a decision.

work_items.title: We prepare the report sent upward from the published numbers
work_items.description: We build the national report from the same registers we published locally.
work_items.prompt: Produce the return from the ledger and the published results instead of retyping it, and keep the version that was sent, with the date it was sent. Where the return asks for data the council has not yet published locally, publish it locally too: a number that is good enough for the national level is good enough for the neighbourhood it comes from. Where the two truly differ, record the reason on the return itself. The AI role may only draft, summarise, remind or count; anything that goes before the public is always approved by a person.

work_items.title: Let us count what the neighbourhoods brought in the past month
work_items.description: Let us compile, by neighbourhood, what came in between the two rounds.
work_items.prompt: Collect last month's reports by Óváros, Kertváros, Malomsor and Határrét, and count by topic how many people reported the same thing. Also note which neighbourhood sent nothing, because that is where the most personal invitation will have to go. The AI role (RU-AI-1) may only count and summarise; a person approves the tally before anything goes before the public.
work_items.form_name: Let us count what the neighbourhoods brought in the past month

work_items.title: Let us word the monthly invitation for each neighbourhood
work_items.description: Let us write the notice that asks what the neighbourhood would like to put on the agenda.
work_items.prompt: Based on the numbers, write a separate invitation for each neighbourhood: say what we heard last month and ask what they would like to bring to the next council meeting. It should include how to respond without an account, and by when. The AI role (RU-AI-1) may only draft and summarise; a person approves the text, and nothing goes out until then.
work_items.form_name: Let us word the monthly invitation for each neighbourhood

work_items.title: Let us approve and post the notice in every neighbourhood
work_items.description: A named person approves the invitation and then posts it.
work_items.prompt: The Communications officer reads all four invitations through, checks the numbers and the deadline, and posts them on the neighbourhood notice boards and the channels. The AI role (RU-AI-1) may not post a notice; a person approves every copy before it goes out, and the approver's name is recorded.
work_items.form_name: Let us approve and post the notice in every neighbourhood

work_items.title: Let us go where the notice does not reach
work_items.description: Let us seek out in person those who do not respond online.
work_items.prompt: Alongside the posted invitation, the Community liaison goes to the neighbourhoods that reported least: to the community house, the market, the seniors' club in Malomsor, and takes down by word of mouth what people say. The AI role (RU-AI-1) may at most draft a reminder for the liaison and summarise their notes; a person approves the report taken down before it is recorded.
work_items.form_name: Let us go where the notice does not reach

work_items.title: Let us count the answers and show which neighbourhood stayed silent
work_items.description: Let us tally the responses to the invitation by neighbourhood.
work_items.prompt: At the end of the month we count how many responded in each neighbourhood and name those from which nothing came, so that the next invitation goes there in a more targeted way. The tally is the basis for the next round's questions. The AI role (RU-AI-1) may only count and summarise; a person approves the publication.
work_items.form_name: Let us count the answers and show which neighbourhood stayed silent

work_items.title: The audit committee chair designates the promises that are expiring
work_items.description: The list of promises coming due is started by the audit committee chair.
work_items.prompt: Based on the council's resolutions and the reports of the consultation rounds, the Audit committee chair selects the promises whose deadline falls in the month (for example the renovation of the Óváros market square or the building of the pavement in Malomsor), and names the responsible role for each. The AI role (RU-AI-1) may prepare a reminder and a count of the approaching deadlines; a person approves the list before anything becomes public.
work_items.form_name: The audit committee chair designates the promises that are expiring

work_items.title: We gather what we heard about the promise
work_items.description: For each promise we gather the reports received from residents and the result of the related round.
work_items.prompt: From the rounds and reports belonging to the promise, the Data and analysis officer counts for each neighbourhood (Óváros, Kertváros, Malomsor, Határrét) how many people reported, and names the neighbourhoods from which nothing came. The AI role (RU-AI-1) may only summarise or count; a person approves the tally before it moves on.
work_items.form_name: We gather what we heard about the promise

work_items.title: The town clerk checks whether the promise was fulfilled
work_items.description: The town clerk establishes from the documents what was delivered of the promise and what it cost (HUF).
work_items.prompt: Based on the documents, contracts and payments (amounts in forints), the Town clerk compares the promise with what was actually completed, and marks it: fulfilled, partly fulfilled or not fulfilled. The AI role (RU-AI-1) may only draft the comparison or send a reminder to the person responsible; a person approves the marking.
work_items.form_name: The town clerk checks whether the promise was fulfilled

work_items.title: We write the plain-language account of the promise
work_items.description: The communications officer writes up what we heard and what it changed.
work_items.prompt: The Communications officer writes one short, plain-language text for each promise: what we promised, what we heard from residents, what changed as a result, and what marking the promise received. The AI role (RU-AI-1) may only draft; a person approves the text before it appears anywhere.
work_items.form_name: We write the plain-language account of the promise

work_items.title: The mayor approves and publishes the marking
work_items.description: The mayor carries out the last step: they approve it and say it in public.
work_items.prompt: The Mayor reviews the markings of the promises and the return, amends it if necessary, and approves it by name. After publication, the register records which promise received which marking and when. An AI does not perform this step; only material approved by a person may go before the public (RU-AI-1).
work_items.form_name: The mayor approves and publishes the marking

work_items.title: Let us accept the request and identify the requester
work_items.description: Let us log the application and make sure it is that very person asking.
work_items.prompt: A request may come from anywhere – by letter, at the office window, at the market from the community liaison, or online – even without an account. We give a case number, record the day of arrival and the deadline for answering, and make sure the requester really is the person whose record is in question (a resident of Óváros, Kertváros, Malomsor or Határrét); we ask for no more than that takes. The AI role (RU-AI-1) may only summarise the request, calculate the deadline and draft a reminder; a person approves the identification and the recording of the deadline.
work_items.form_name: Let us accept the request and identify the requester

work_items.title: Let us gather what the register holds about us
work_items.description: Let us find, in every source, what we hold about the applicant.
work_items.prompt: From the register, the electoral roll, the business and market lists, the departments' mailing lists and the answers to the consultation rounds, gather into one place everything that belongs to the requester, marking each source. Anything that matches only uncertainly is not counted as the requester's but marked separately. The AI role (RU-AI-1) may only summarise the matches and count the records per source; a person approves what belongs to the requester.
work_items.form_name: Let us gather what the register holds about us

work_items.title: Let us decide what we release, and what we cannot delete
work_items.description: Let us separate what can be released, what can be deleted, and what must be kept because of the law.
work_items.prompt: Decide record by record whether it can be released, whether it can be deleted, or whether it must be kept because of a legal or records-retention obligation. If we do not delete something, we write down the answer and the reason rather than staying silent. The AI role (RU-AI-1) may only summarise the retention rules and draft a proposal; a person approves the decision, and a person also approves carrying out the deletion.
work_items.form_name: Let us decide what we release, and what we cannot delete

work_items.title: Let us prepare the reply and the copy to be released
work_items.description: Let us draft the reply and put together a copy of the data.
work_items.prompt: From the accepted decision, put together a plain-language reply and a readable copy of the data. Say what we found, what we are releasing, what we deleted or why we did not, and where the requester can turn with a complaint. The AI role (RU-AI-1) may only draft the text of the letter and the copy; a named person approves the outgoing material before anything leaves the office.
work_items.form_name: Let us prepare the reply and the copy to be released

work_items.title: Let us send the dated reply and note what happened
work_items.description: Let us hand over the reply and close the application with a note for the record.
work_items.prompt: Send the approved reply in the way the requester asked, and record the date, the deletion or release carried out, and who approved it. The record must not contain more personal data than necessary. Every month, count the closed requests by neighbourhood and the replies that came after the deadline. The AI role (RU-AI-1) may only summarise, count and draft reminders about expiring deadlines; a person approves the closing of the record.
work_items.form_name: Let us send the dated reply and note what happened

work_items.title: We select the decision to examine and the question
work_items.description: The audit committee chair names the decision and writes down what they want to find out.
work_items.prompt: The Audit committee chair selects a council decision that has already been recorded, for example the resolution on the renovation of the Malomsor Market Square, and writes the question in one sentence: did the decision reflect what residents said in the consultation round. They record the decision's case number and the deadline for the review, and put it before the council so that the review is public. A person performs this step; there is no AI role in it.
work_items.form_name: We select the decision to examine and the question

work_items.title: We count what we heard before the decision
work_items.description: The data and analysis officer counts, by neighbourhood, the responses that preceded the decision.
work_items.prompt: From the answers of the round belonging to the decision, the Data and analysis officer counts by neighbourhood (Óváros, Kertváros, Malomsor, Határrét) how many people said what, and gives the denominator: how many people were asked and how many answered. They name the missing neighbourhoods and do not leave them out. The AI role (RU-AI-1) may only summarise and count; a person approves material that goes before the public.
work_items.form_name: We count what we heard before the decision

work_items.title: We compare the decision with what we heard
work_items.description: The town clerk compares the recorded decision point by point with the opinions heard.
work_items.prompt: The Town clerk takes out the text of the decision and the proposal and compares them point by point with the counted answers: what the decision adopted, what it rejected, and for a rejected point, what the reason was. The comparison is written with reference to the original documents, not from memory. The AI role (RU-AI-1) may only draft the comparison; a person approves material that goes before the public.
work_items.form_name: We compare the decision with what we heard

work_items.title: We write down the finding
work_items.description: The audit committee chair records what they found in their own words.
work_items.prompt: Based on the comparison, the Audit committee chair writes the finding: what we heard, what this changed in the decision and what it did not, and states it if a promise remained unfulfilled. Where the committee lacks enough data, that too is written down. The chair writes and signs the finding; no AI role drafts it for them.
work_items.form_name: We write down the finding

work_items.title: The council responds to the finding
work_items.description: The mayor answers the finding on behalf of the council and says what will change.
work_items.prompt: The Mayor / council chair has the finding discussed at the council's meeting and answers: whether it is accepted, what is changed in the decision, and by when at the latest, with the amount in forints if it carries a cost (for example 4 800 000 Ft for the additional works on the market square). The answer becomes a recorded council document. The AI role (RU-AI-1) may only draft the answer and draft reminders about the deadlines; a person approves material that goes before the public.
work_items.form_name: The council responds to the finding

work_items.title: We publish the review, the finding and the response
work_items.description: The communications officer publishes the three documents to those who responded.
work_items.prompt: The Communications officer publishes the review, the finding and the council's answer together, and sends them to the residents and groups who answered in the round, by neighbourhood and in their own language: what we heard and what changed because of it. They do not send the outgoing material until the Audit committee chair and the mayor have approved it. The AI role (RU-AI-1) may only draft the notice, summarise and follow up on who it did not reach; a person approves material that goes before the public.
work_items.form_name: We publish the review, the finding and the response

work_items.title: We show in which neighbourhoods the register is thin
work_items.description: Let us count, by neighbourhood, how many people are in the register compared with the expected population.
